nameStory: The common white-cheeked jumping spider gets its name from the distinctive white or pale markings that appear like little 'cheeks' on the sides of its head region. These bright patches stand out against its darker body, making it look like it's sporting fashionable face paint that helps naturalists spot it among the foliage.
description: The common white-cheeked jumping spider is a tiny, athletic hunter that prowls through gardens and wild spaces across New England. These compact spiders have sturdy, somewhat flattened bodies with relatively short, powerful legs built for quick jumps rather than long-distance running. Males are quite small at about 3-4mm long (roughly the size of a peppercorn), while females are noticeably larger at 4-6mm. Like all jumping spiders, they have excellent vision and actively stalk their prey rather than building webs to catch insects.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive white or cream-colored patches on the sides of the head region that give this spider its 'white-cheeked' name - these pale markings contrast sharply with the darker body

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes arranged in a row across the front of the face, with the two center eyes noticeably larger and giving an almost cartoon-like appearance

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, somewhat flattened body with a relatively large head region (cephalothorax) compared to the rounded abdomen - feels firm and solid if gently handled

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Quite small - males about the size of a peppercorn, females closer to a small pea, making them one of the smaller jumping spiders you'll encounter

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with sudden stops, often raising its front legs and turning to face you directly when approached - no web building

habitat: Common white-cheeked jumping spiders thrive in a variety of habitats including gardens, forest edges, meadows, and brushy areas throughout New England. They're often found on low vegetation, wooden fences, building exteriors, and among leaf litter where they hunt for small insects. Look for them on sunny surfaces where they can bask while watching for prey.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, with mating displays beginning. Males may be seen performing elaborate courtship dances with leg waving and body movements.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both males and females are most commonly observed hunting. This is the best time to spot their distinctive white cheek markings.
seasonality.fall: Females lay egg sacs in protected locations. Adults remain active until first frost, often seen sunning themselves on warm surfaces during cooler days.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with the species overwintering as juveniles or in egg sacs tucked into bark crevices and other protected spots.

funFact: When threatened, common white-cheeked jumping spiders can leap more than 10 times their own body length in a single bound - imagine if you could jump across an entire basketball court in one hop!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small jumping spiders in the Pelegrina genus, but the distinctive white cheek patches are usually diagnostic. Memory trick: 'White cheeks = white-cheeked' - if you can't see pale markings on the sides of the head, you're probably looking at a different species.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Pelegrina comes from Latin meaning 'wandering' or 'traveling,' which perfectly captures these spiders' active hunting lifestyle as they roam through their territories rather than sitting in webs waiting for prey to come to them.
compareHints: Among its Pelegrina relatives in New England, the white-cheeked jumping spider is distinguished by those prominent pale cheek markings - the peppered jumping spider has more scattered light spots, while the yellowleg jumping spider has distinctly yellow-colored legs. The white cheek patches are really this species' signature feature that sets it apart from its close cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Pelegrina relatives, the Peppered Jumping Spider is distinguished by its speckled 'peppered' pattern rather than the white facial markings of the White-cheeked Jumping Spider or the yellow coloration of the Yellowleg Jumping Spider.
